Title: Bootstrapping and OOB samples in Random Forests | by Divya Choudhary | Analytics Vidhya | Medium
Analytics Vidhya is a community of Generative AI and Data Science professionals. # Bootstrapping and OOB samples in Random Forests. If you have read about Bootstrap and Out of Bag (OOB) samples in Random Forest (RF), you would most certainly have read that the fraction of observations in the ‘bag’ when you build RF with bootstrap is around 63.2%. **Bootstrap** means that instead of training on all the observations, each tree of RF is trained on a subset of the observations. Multiple trees are trained on different bags, and later the results from all the trees are **aggregated**. If we have 1000 training observations, then for every bag, a set of 1000 observations are selected from the training set. This process is repeated 1000 times for Bag1. So its quite possible that there will be repetitions in the observations that make it to the bag. All the observations that do not make it to the Bag1 are called the OOB for Bag1. Multiple such Bags are created for training multiple trees. The number of observations in training set = n. Probability of an observation being selected in a draw = 1/n. Probability of an observation not being selected in a draw = 1-(1/n). Number of draws = Size of Bag = n. Therefore, the probability of an observation not being selected in all the draws for Bag1 = [1-(1/n)]^n. Probability of an observation making it into the bag after n draws. As the value of n increases the Prob of OOB saturates at .368, and correspondingly the Prob of samples in the bag at .632. By training multiple trees on multiple such bootstrapped samples in combination with other parameters like column sampling, each tree gets visibility of a region of the observation space, and thus multiple uncorrelated trees are created. ## The average bootstrap sample omits 36.8% of the data.
